title: Market failure: externalities, common pool resources and public goods
summary: Markets over- or under-produce when costs or benefits fall on third parties, when shared resources are overused, and when public goods face the free-rider problem. Governments respond with taxes, subsidies, regulation, permits, provision and cooperation.

keyterms.definition: When the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently, so output is not where MSB = MSC.
A cost or benefit of production or consumption that affects third parties not involved in the transaction.

keyterms.term: Marginal social cost and benefit (MSC, MSB)
keyterms.definition: The full cost or benefit to society of one more unit: private plus external.
External costs from producing a good, e.g. pollution from a factory; MSC > MPC, so the good is overproduced.
External costs from consuming a good, e.g. passive smoking; MSB < MPB, so the good is overconsumed.
External benefits from consumption, e.g. vaccinations; MSB > MPB, so the good is underconsumed.
External benefits from production, e.g. staff training used by other firms; MSC < MPC, so underproduced.
A good that benefits users and society more than people realise, so it is underconsumed, e.g. education.
A good more harmful to users and society than people realise, so it is overconsumed, e.g. tobacco.
A tax equal to the external cost per unit, which shifts MPC up to MSC to internalise the externality.
A cap on total pollution with permits that firms can buy and sell, so cuts are made where they are cheapest.
A resource that is rivalrous but non-excludable, such as fish stocks, so it tends to be overused.
Overuse and depletion of a common pool resource because each user ignores the cost imposed on others.
A good that is non-rivalrous and non-excludable, e.g. street lighting or national defence.
People can benefit from a public good without paying, so private firms cannot profitably supply it.
Communities managing shared resources through their own rules and monitoring, as studied by Elinor Ostrom.

questions.prompt: A paper mill pollutes a river used by fishers. In the paper market…
options: MSB > MPB, so paper is underproduced
MSC < MPC, so paper is underproduced
MSC > MPC, so paper is overproduced
questions.explanation: The pollution is an external cost; ignoring it, the market produces beyond the social optimum.

questions.statement: Vaccinations generate a positive consumption externality because vaccinated people reduce the spread of disease to others.
questions.explanation: MSB > MPB, so the free market underconsumes vaccines.

questions.prompt: Match each example to the type of externality.

pairs.left: A beekeeper’s bees pollinate nearby orchards

questions.explanation: Ask: who causes the spillover (producer or consumer) and is it a cost or benefit?

questions.text: A good that is underconsumed because people underestimate its benefits is a ___ good.
questions.explanation: Merit goods are often linked to positive consumption externalities and imperfect information.

questions.prompt: Which policy best internalises a negative production externality?
options: A tax per unit equal to the external cost
questions.explanation: A Pigouvian tax raises MPC to MSC, so output falls to the social optimum.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of tradable permits over command-and-control regulation?
options: Pollution is cut by the firms that can do so most cheaply
questions.explanation: Firms with low abatement costs cut more and sell permits; the cap still fixes total emissions.

questions.statement: A carbon tax gives firms an ongoing incentive to cut emissions.
questions.explanation: Every tonne avoided saves tax, encouraging cleaner technology.

questions.text: The welfare loss from a negative externality arises because output is above the level where MSB = ___.
questions.explanation: The allocatively efficient output is where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost.

questions.prompt: Which is the best policy to increase consumption of a merit good like preventive health checks?
options: A subsidy or free provision, plus information campaigns
questions.explanation: Lowering the price and correcting information gaps both raise consumption towards the optimum.

questions.prompt: Order the effects of a carbon tax.
items: Tax raises the cost of emitting
Firms’ supply shifts left (MPC rises towards MSC)
questions.explanation: A Pigouvian tax internalises the externality and raises revenue.

lessons.title: Common pool resources and public goods

questions.prompt: Why are ocean fish stocks a common pool resource?
options: They are rivalrous but hard to exclude people from
They are produced by the government
questions.explanation: One boat’s catch leaves fewer fish for others, but stopping boats from fishing is hard.

questions.text: Overuse of a shared resource because users ignore costs imposed on others is the tragedy of the ___.
questions.explanation: Rational individual choices lead to collective depletion.

questions.statement: A lighthouse is a classic example of a public good.
questions.explanation: One ship using the light does not reduce it for others, and ships cannot easily be excluded.

questions.prompt: Why does the free market fail to provide public goods?
options: Public goods are always too expensive to produce
Demand for public goods is zero
People can benefit without paying (free riding), so firms cannot earn revenue
questions.explanation: Non-excludability creates the free-rider problem, so there is a "missing market".

questions.prompt: Match each good to its classification.
questions.explanation: Rivalry and excludability decide the category.

questions.prompt: Elinor Ostrom showed that common pool resources can be managed sustainably by…
options: local communities setting and enforcing their own rules
questions.explanation: Collective self-governance can work where users communicate, monitor and sanction rule-breakers.

questions.statement: Climate change requires international cooperation because the atmosphere is a global common pool resource.
questions.explanation: No single country can solve it; each faces incentives to free ride on others’ cuts.

questions.text: Goods that are non-rivalrous and non-excludable are ___ goods.
questions.explanation: Pure public goods are usually funded by taxes.

options: A subsidy for fuel for fishing boats
questions.explanation: Quotas cap the amount taken. Fuel subsidies would encourage more fishing.

questions.prompt: Order the tragedy of the commons for a shared pasture.
items: Each herder adds animals to gain more
Total grazing exceeds the pasture’s regeneration
questions.explanation: Individual incentives conflict with collective sustainability.
